extracted.intended_audience: architects, auditorium designers, builders, and acoustical engineers (or practitioners concerned with designing/retrofitting speaking/music halls)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical design and retrofitting guidance for achieving good acoustic properties in auditoria, focusing on air conditions, wall materials and arrangement, room shape, ventilation, and speaker/reflector treatment. Geared toward design decisions that minimize reverberation, echoes, and indistinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of the air (homogeneity vs currents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion of the air within an auditorium (whether it is quiet and mechanically homogeneous or contains mingled draughts of hot and cold air moving in various directions) exercises a very perceptible effect on its acoustic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneous, quiet air transmits sounds readily; alternating convection-currents of warm and cold air (mechanically heterogeneous air) produce partial reflections at each density variation, creating a multitude of secondary waves that mask the direct sound and cause indistinctness and confusion. Examples/anti-patterns: Sounds heard clearly across a calm mile (homogeneous air) vs. shouts confused within a hundred feet in post-fire heterogenous air. Design implication: avoid establishing alternating small air-currents within the hall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation strategy to avoid disruptive currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Ventilate by admitting air in large volume and at the proper temperature and carrying it bodily across the room in one large mass as nearly as may be without breaking homogeneity, then exhaust at the opposite side; or introduce through a perforated floor and exhaust at the roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implementations: bring fresh air to proper temperature in the basement, pass it through many small holes upward, and exhaust at the ceiling/tower (example: Baltimore Academy of Music). Avoid many small localized registers or open windows that create alternating currents and counter-currents. Aim for gentle bulk flow to prevent formation of minor air-currents that degrade intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid small localized ventilation currents within the occupied space
rubrics_metrics.description: Registers, sprinkled over the floor, and open windows or cold-air ventilators produce hot and cold currents that do not readily mix and fill the auditorium with alternations in temperature, density, and relative motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: scattered registers and open doors producing counter-currents; observed effect: marked deterioration in intelligibility during periods of disrupted circulation (experimental notes from observers in Baltimore Academy of Music). Design response: centralize and smooth air supply/exhaust to minimize localized currents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walls should absorb, not reflect, stray sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls must be built of such material and arranged in such a way that they shall absorb and not reflect sound-waves falling upon them; stray rays of sound (those not going directly to listeners) should be as completely as possible absorbed and destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: reflected stray rays arriving later than direct sound bridge syllables together causing indistinct articulation. Practical measures: avoid large blank reflective surfaces opposite the speaker; use absorbent linings, drapery, or paneling to remove waste sound. Audience presence absorbs some floor-reflected sound but cannot substitute for wall absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorptive power of wall materials (ranked list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different wall materials vary greatly in absorptive power; the author measured absorptive power by coupling vibrating tuning-forks to walls and observing emitted sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking (most to least absorptive) as reported: 1. Thin and dry pine sheathing, lightly supported or in panels. 2. Corrugated iron. 3. Heavy wood paneling. 4. Thin, dry, hard plaster on light laths, lightly suspended. 5. Heavy plaster on laths lightly supported or attached to wooden walls. 6. Heavy plaster on laths closely fitted to brick/stone. 7. Thin brick walls. 8. Thin brick walls covered with plaster directly laid on. 9. Thick brick walls. 10. Marble and other stone walls. Guidance: prefer materials high on this list for lining; experimental data corresponds with observed performance in churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use corrugated iron and thin wooden linings where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrugated iron has very good absorptive power for sound while being durable, fire-safe, and amenable to ornamentation; thin pine-wood sheathing, lightly suspended with a free air-space behind, will absorb sound very completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bethany Church (Baltimore) built of corrugated iron is an acoustic success. Practical approach: when main walls must be stone or brick, recover acoustic qualities by lining with thin pine, corrugated iron, or thin plaster on light laths suspended as lightly as possible and at significant distance from solid wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall arrangement: spacing, light suspension, and paneling
rubrics_metrics.description: Lining of walls should be placed at a considerable distance from the main wall and supported to allow as free vibration as possible; arrangement of walls in panels is advantageous so each panel can vibrate easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal: brick or stone outer walls with an inner shell of thin wooden panels set at sufficient distance to permit passageways and free vibration (improves absorption). Avoid linings closely fitted to solid walls (reduces absorptive effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid large blank walls; break up reflecting surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain blank wall opposite the speaker will throw back strong reverberation; if broken up by recesses, pilasters, or galleries, reverberation is much less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tactics: use recesses, pilasters, extended galleries, or paneling to interrupt large reflective surfaces. When rooms must be square/oblong, take great care to avoid large reflecting surfaces and use devices to absorb waste sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred auditorium shape: ovate/egg-shell section
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper shape of an auditorium is, in general, that of an egg-shell, the speaker being at the focus of the smaller end and the audience seated over the lower half while the upper half forms the vaulted roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: open-air assemblies and amphitheatres show good sound distribution; egg-shape yields floor curving upward from speaker, galleries as continuation, and natural diffusion to absorb stray rays. While ideal, departures are often necessary; if other shapes are used, ensure materials and air condition are controlled to achieve acoustic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for concave vaulted roofs and their focusing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaulted roofs of proper curvature and of non-absorbing material can act as concave mirrors gathering waste rays and reflecting them back to a focus in the audience, producing a loud and disagreeable echo (focus may be area or line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies: select absorbing materials for the roof, change curvature, break the roof by transverse arches, replace the ceiling in severe cases, or reposition the pulpit to alter focal relationships. Use reflectors/sounding-boards cautiously to mitigate roof focusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflectors/sounding-boards only with judicious care
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflectors' object is not to gather rays and throw them to a focus (which can do more harm than good), but to control rays that would otherwise go up to the roof and be retained as a disagreeable echo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective design: a flat surface placed over the pulpit and not too far from the speaker's head can prevent sound going to the roof; better: have the wall behind the pulpit gradually curve forward to overhang the speaker so direct and reflected sounds are as nearly identical as possible. Avoid large concave reflectors that produce a distant focus and strong echoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit placement and small-scale reflectors as remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: In buildings with problematic ceilings or vaulting, moving the pulpit near one corner or against a wall half-way down a side often alleviates focusing faults; small near reflectors can throw sound toward the audience and prevent it going up to the roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full ceiling replacement is impractical, try pulpit repositioning or adding a near reflector/sounding-board. Ensure the speaker is close enough to the reflector so direct and reflected sounds are nearly identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and drapery as partial absorbers but not substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of an audience causes absorption of words that would otherwise be reflected from the floor and walls, but it is out of the question to cover walls with an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While draping heavily with cloth can help absorption, experiments show other materials (e.g., thin pine sheathing, corrugated iron) handled more conveniently answer the purpose better. Design should not rely on the audience to solve wall-reflection problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence for harmonic proportions of room dimensions as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that a hall must have its length, breadth, and height in harmonic proportion to be acoustically good has no good foundation; careful experimental inquiry failed to find this to be the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize simple harmonic dimensional ratios over the more important factors: air condition, wall materials/arrangement, shape and surface treatment. Focus on controlling reflections and air homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker technique: timing (the 'key-note') in resonant rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: In rooms with considerable resonance, a speaker can often be understood by timing syllables so that the resonance of one has disappeared before the next is uttered; the 'key-note' concept relates more to syllable timing than to pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional note for performers/speakers: adjust speaking rate and syllable timing to accommodate room resonance. This is a behavioral mitigation when architectural remedies are limited.
